content: Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) is a severe and life-threatening condition associated with high rates of mortality and morbidity. Aerosolized prostacyclin has been utilized in clinical settings to improve oxygenation in patients with ARDS, although the evidence supporting its efficacy remains limited. This review, initially published in 2010 and updated in 2017, aimed to evaluate the potential benefits and harms of aerosolized prostacyclin in both adult and pediatric populations with ARDS. To conduct this review, a comprehensive search was performed across multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, ISI BIOSIS Previews, ISI Web of Science, LILACS, and CINAHL, as well as three clinical trial registries. The search covered all available studies up to May 5, 2017. Additionally, reference lists of relevant reviews, trials, and editorials were manually examined, and study authors were contacted to identify any unpublished, ongoing, or missing data. The inclusion criteria encompassed all randomized controlled trials (RCTs), regardless of publication status, language, or blinding. Three independent reviewers extracted data from the included studies, resolving any disagreements through discussion. The primary outcome of interest was all-cause mortality. Subgroup and sensitivity analyses were planned to evaluate the effects of aerosolized prostacyclin in different populations (adults versus children) and on various clinical and physiological outcomes. The risk of bias was assessed by examining the methodological quality of the trials, and the risk of random error was evaluated using trial sequential analysis. The review included two RCTs with a total of 81 participants. One trial involved 14 critically ill children with ARDS, while the other included 67 critically ill adults. Both studies were assessed as providing very low-quality evidence. The pediatric trial reported no significant difference in mortality between the intervention and control groups, but its cross-over design limited its contribution to meta-analysis. The adult trial found no significant improvement in the partial pressure of oxygen in arterial blood to the fraction of inspired oxygen (PaO2/FiO2) ratio, with a mean difference of -25.35 (95% confidence interval: -60.48 to 9.78; P = 0.16). No adverse events, such as bleeding or organ dysfunction, were reported in either trial. Due to the small number of included studies, the planned subgroup and sensitivity analyses, as well as trial sequential analysis, could not be performed. The results were too imprecise to determine whether aerosolized prostacyclin has a meaningful effect on mortality. Consequently, there is currently no evidence to support or refute the routine use of aerosolized prostacyclin in patients with ARDS. The authors emphasize the urgent need for additional high-quality RCTs to better understand the potential role of this intervention in ARDS management.
